title: New Breathalyser Detects Fat Burning in Real Time From a Single Breath
excerpt: Researchers at ETH Zurich have developed a handheld device that measures breath acetone with laboratory-grade accuracy in 90 seconds, offering a new way to track metabolism during exercise, fasting, and dieting.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • ETH Zurich's breathalyser detects fat burning by measuring acetone in a single breath.
  • Device tested on 12 volunteers, matching lab-grade accuracy in 90 seconds.
  • Commercialized as 'Nutrion', it's used in clinical trials for various health conditions.
  • Technology could replace invasive blood tests for monitoring ketosis at home.

A compact breathalyser that can tell whether your body is burning fat from a single exhalation has been developed by researchers at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (ETH) in Zurich. The device delivers laboratory-grade acetone readings in roughly 90 seconds and could transform how people monitor metabolism during weight loss, fasting, or athletic training.

The findings, published July 22 in the journal Device, describe a smartphone-assisted detector that measures breath acetone — a volatile compound released when the body breaks down fatty acids during ketosis. When carbohydrate supplies run low, the body shifts to burning stored fat, producing ketones in the liver. Acetone is a byproduct of that process and passes into the breath.

Laboratory Accuracy in a Handheld Device

Consumer breath-testing devices already exist, but many struggle to deliver reliable readings. Humidity, variations in breathing technique, and chemically similar compounds such as alcohol can interfere with sensors. Blood-ketone tests offer more accuracy but require repeated finger pricks, and clinical tools like MRI body composition scans demand a hospital visit.

The ETH Zurich team, led by senior author Andreas Güntner and first author Simone Hersberger, combined an acetone-specific chemical sensor with miniature filters that strip out moisture and interfering compounds before measurement. A paired smartphone app coaches users through a controlled exhalation, capturing acetone at the point when breath levels most closely reflect bloodstream concentrations.

"If we want to make that information available to patients, we need to shrink those technologies into compact, user-friendly devices."

— Andreas Güntner, ETH Zurich

Strong Results in a Small Trial

The team tested the device on 12 healthy adults under real-world conditions, collecting 312 breath samples with acetone concentrations ranging from 0.2 to 45 parts per million. Readings closely matched those from proton transfer reaction time-of-flight mass spectrometry (PTR-MS), the gold standard for breath analysis.

Participants were monitored under four metabolic conditions: light exercise followed by a high-carbohydrate meal, intense exercise followed by a high-carb meal, a fat-rich ketogenic meal, and fasting. Breath acetone stayed low after light exercise and carbohydrates but rose sharply following intense workouts, dropping again when participants consumed sugary foods.

"We were able to resolve even the finest changes in breath as someone started to burn fat," Güntner told New Scientist. "After more intensive exercise, we saw breath acetone increase, but if someone then drank a sugary drink or ate a carbohydrate-rich meal, we could see it immediately fall again."

Beyond Weight Loss

The device has been commercialised by Alivion AG, an ETH Zurich spin-off, under the brand name Nutrion. Two of the paper's authors, including Güntner, are shareholders in the company, and ETH Zurich holds the underlying patent.

Nutrion is now being used in clinical trials that extend well beyond weight management. Ketogenic diets are an established treatment for some forms of drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly in children, but monitoring adherence currently requires repeated blood draws. An ongoing trial is evaluating whether Nutrion can replace that burden with a simple breath test. The device is also being investigated alongside intermittent fasting protocols, GLP-1 weight-loss therapies such as semaglutide, and ketogenic diets during cancer treatment.

"We're really moving toward health care solutions that, in the future, you won't need to go to the hospital for anymore. You'll be able to do them at home."

— Andreas Güntner, ETH Zurich
Nutrion's Clinical Applications

Independent expert Dirk Dugdale-Duwell of Elevate Performance Testing in the UK called the epilepsy work promising, noting it "would take some logistical strain off home testing for blood-ketone monitoring." He added that athletes might use the device to tailor carbohydrate intake to real-time metabolic data, though performance benefits remain unproven.

The study's main limitation is its small sample size — 12 healthy adults. The researchers acknowledge the device needs validation in larger, more diverse populations, including people with metabolic disorders. For the millions managing diabetes and obesity worldwide — including India's diabetic population of more than 100 million — a non-invasive, real-time metabolic monitor could eventually reduce reliance on blood tests and clinic visits.
